> 既濟。亨，小利貞。初吉，終亂。

Hexagram 63 is about having crossed, and its first character is the word for having finished a meal.

## 既: the bowl is empty and the person looks back

既: already, done. The oracle-bone form is a person who has finished eating, turning to look back.

濟: to cross (說文 gives it as a river name; the classics borrow it for crossing).

So 既濟 is not "victory." It is: the crossing is done, the bowl is empty, and one turns round.

Which means the two words already carry the coolness of the judgement: 初吉，終亂 — good at first, disordered at the end.

## 曳其輪，濡其尾

初九: pull back on the wheel; the tail gets wet; no fault.

曳: to drag. 濡: to soak.

Which is the posture of the hexagram's first line: having crossed, deliberately slowing the wheels, and getting the tail wet in the process — and that being no fault, because one did not charge ahead.

And the top line repeats 濡 with the other end: 濡其首 — the head wet, and there is no going on. Same character, two lines, one light and one fatal.

## 婦喪其茀，勿逐，七日得

茀: originally "the road grown over with grass" (說文 茀，道多草不可行); here the carriage screen, the curtain on a woman's cart.

Which matters: the curtain is not decoration. It is cover — it shades the outside and shelters the inside.

So losing the 茀 is not losing an object. It is losing the layer of cover.

And the advice is 勿逐 — do not chase. Seven days, and it comes back. The third appearance of that period in this book (復, 震, here), and the same content every time: what was lost in a crossing is recovered by waiting, not by pursuit.

## 繻有衣袽，終日戒

繻: fine, closely woven silk (說文 繻，繒采色).
袽: worn-out clothing, old wadding.

六四: 繻有衣袽，終日戒.

Which is one of the hardest sentences in the book, and its point is simple: even the finest silk, left lying, becomes worn wadding.

Nobody tore it. Time did.

Hence 終日戒 — on guard all day. Not against an enemy. Against the fact that a finished thing starts to fray the moment it is finished.

## 東鄰殺牛，不如西鄰之禴祭

九五: the eastern neighbour slaughters an ox, and it is not as good as the western neighbour's 禴 sacrifice, which truly receives the blessing.

禴: the summer sacrifice, the thinnest of the four seasonal rites — new vegetables only.

And the key to 禴 is not "thin." It is "timely": at that season, offering what has just grown is the full rite.

So nine-five is not saying "cheap is better." It is saying "in season is better" — the ox out of season is worth less than the vegetables in season.

Which is the whole hexagram in one image: 既濟 is the state where abundance has been achieved and timing has not.

## 高宗伐鬼方，三年克之

Nine-three: the high ancestor campaigns against the Gui region, and it takes three years to subdue.

三年 — three years, stated twice in the book (here and 未濟九四).

So even the hexagram of completion measures its hardest work in years, and adds 小人勿用 — do not use small men for it.

## 思患而預防之

The 象: 君子以思患而預防之 — think of the trouble and prevent it beforehand.

Which is the only advice available in a hexagram about having arrived: nothing can be added, so the work becomes maintenance.

## The test

Take something finished — a launch, a project, a recovery. Ask the fourth line's question: what is fraying while nothing is happening to it? And the fifth's: is this the ox out of season, or the vegetables in season?
